title: Bond Relief, Soft Jobs and AI Memory
summary: George and Alice cover the week to 6 October 2026: record US equity highs, lingering gilt and Treasury risks, softer US payrolls and a modestly better UK growth picture. They also discuss Micron’s exceptional AI-memory results, Nike’s still-messy turnaround, and the key market events coming next.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: US stocks hit fresh highs, but the bond market is still breathing down everyone’s neck.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Hello and welcome to The Weekly Market Brief, covering Tuesday the twenty ninth of September to Tuesday the sixth of October, just after seven p.m. UK time. I’m George.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And I’m Alice. Quick reminder: this is general market information, not personal financial advice. Do your own research, because we don’t know your ISA, your mortgage, or your tolerance for chaos.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Right. Story one: yields, oil and AI. On the sixth of October, US equities rebounded, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq reaching records, helped by lower Treasury yields, lower oil, and continuing AI optimism.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes, but earlier in the week, sovereign yields were under pressure. The Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee said gilt and US Treasury yields had reached levels not seen since 2008, and hedge-fund leverage in gilts remained elevated.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So lower yields help growth shares, but the warning hasn’t gone away.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. A renewed rise in long yields would be a headwind for equity valuations, duration-heavy bond funds and mortgage-sensitive sectors. Relief rally, not clean bill of health.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Oil helped too. OPEC said seven countries, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, would keep November production at September-required levels.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And Reuters reported prices slipped as Middle East crude exports increased and the G7 pledged additional supply releases. Helpful for airlines, logistics and inflation expectations. But conflict-linked disruption risk is still live.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Second big story: US labour cooled sharply.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Very sharply. September nonfarm payrolls rose by twenty nine thousand. Unemployment was four point two percent, average hourly earnings rose zero point one percent month on month, and July and August payrolls were revised down by sixty thousand combined.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Markets hear that and think: less pressure for a Fed hike in October.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: They do. But softer jobs only help rate-sensitive assets if they don’t become an earnings problem. Banks, staffing, discretionary retail, travel and semiconductors are the areas to watch.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Third story: the UK looked a bit better. The ONS revised Q2 real GDP growth up to zero point five percent, after zero point six percent in Q1.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And real household disposable income per head rose one percent in Q2, after falling zero point eight percent in Q1. Helpful, but not a magic wand.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Because the fiscal and gilt concerns are still there.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. Better household income helps the domestic backdrop, but it doesn’t remove the bond-market risks we started with.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let’s move to earnings. The standout was Micron.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Honestly, extraordinary numbers. Fiscal Q4 revenue was fifty four point two three billion dollars, up from eleven point three two billion a year earlier. GAAP net income was thirty seven point seven billion dollars, and GAAP gross margin was eighty six point eight percent.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That is not your normal memory-cycle print.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: No. Management guided fiscal Q1 2027 revenue to sixty one point five billion dollars, plus or minus one point five billion, with non-GAAP gross margin around eighty six point two five percent.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And the implication?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It’s the clearest earnings evidence this week that AI infrastructure demand is feeding into memory pricing and margins. But memory is historically cyclical. HBM or DRAM oversupply, hyperscaler capex discipline, or customer concentration would matter quickly.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Second earnings name: Nike. Very different tone.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Very different. Fiscal Q1 revenue was eleven point two billion dollars, down four percent reported and five percent currency-neutral. Gross margin improved by sixty basis points to forty two point eight percent, and diluted EPS was forty eight cents.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So cost control is improving, but the turnaround isn’t revenue-led yet.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That’s the issue. Fiscal 2027 revenue is still expected to decline high single digits. Adjusted diluted EPS guidance is one dollar fifteen to one dollar thirty five, excluding about fifteen cents of restructuring expense related to Pace.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Worth a closer look this week: Micron, strictly as a research candidate, not a recommendation.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes. It’s a direct way to study the AI-memory cycle, but the key risk is that current profitability may be unusually high for a commodity-like semiconductor business. Falling HBM prices, inventory build, or capex outrunning free cash flow would weaken the thesis.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Week ahead. Wednesday at one p.m. UK time, Constellation Brands has its Q2 call; the release was scheduled after our cutoff, so it’s upcoming, not reviewed. Then at seven p.m., Fed minutes from September.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Thursday, PepsiCo has Q3 materials at eleven a.m. and analyst Q&A at one fifteen p.m. UK time. Tesco also reports interim results, with UK grocery volumes and price investment in focus.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And Friday at three p.m. UK time, Delta Air Lines’ September-quarter webcast. Useful for fuel, premium travel, corporate demand and free-cash-flow commentary.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Links to the full written briefing and sources are in the show notes. Final reminder: this is general information, not personal financial advice. Do your own research and check suitability before acting.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Thanks for listening to The Weekly Market Brief. We’ll be back next week.
